questions.q: Besides container images, what else might an artifact repository store?
options: Only source code commits
Compiled packages and libraries, and general build outputs like binaries or installer files
Nothing — artifact repositories only ever store container images
User account credentials
questions.explain: Artifact repositories store anything a build process produces that's worth keeping and versioning — images, packages, libraries, and build outputs.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a container registry like GHCR and a package feed like Azure Artifacts?
options: There is no real difference; they are interchangeable terms for the same tool
A container registry specializes in container images; a package feed specializes in libraries and packages like npm or compiled wheels
Package feeds cannot be versioned
Container registries only work with GitHub repositories
questions.explain: Both solve the same underlying problem — versioned artifact storage — but specialize in different artifact types.

questions.q: Why does a registry keeping every previously pushed image version matter for Northbridge Retail?
options: It has no practical benefit, just extra storage use
It makes rollback possible — if a new version breaks, the previous working version is still there, pullable by its own tag
It automatically fixes bugs in older versions
It prevents any new image from ever being pushed again
questions.explain: Because older versions aren't deleted when a newer one is pushed, a known-good previous version remains available to deploy if the new one fails.

questions.q: What risk does deploying from an image tagged `latest` introduce?
options: latest images always run slower
latest is a mutable pointer — a pod restart could silently pull a different image with no corresponding code change or record of what's running
latest tags cannot be pulled by Kubernetes at all
There is no risk; latest is the recommended way to pin a deployment
questions.explain: Because latest gets reassigned on every push, referencing it instead of an immutable tag means what's actually running can change without any traceable event.

questions.q: What does 'pinning' a version mean in the context of artifact repositories?
options: Marking an artifact as a company favorite in the UI
Referencing an exact, immutable version (like a commit SHA tag) instead of a mutable pointer like latest
Deleting all older versions of an artifact
Compressing an artifact to reduce its file size
questions.explain: Pinning means a deployment or dependency references a specific, unchanging version, making 'what's running' an answerable fact rather than a moving target.
